title: Why I'm selling Ethos (LIFE)
subtitle: Revenue grew 151%, but the bottom line stopped keeping up
body:
Ethos grew revenue 24% from Q2 to Q3, from $189.6M to $235.2M. Adjusted EBITDA went from $35.2M to $34.9M. An extra $45.7M of revenue produced slightly less adjusted profit.

That is why I've trimmed LIFE heavily, and I'm leaning toward selling the rest. I haven't fully decided yet, so I'll lay out what changed.

I bought after my May analysis gave it a PASS. Q1 revenue had doubled, it was profitable, and it showed a 98% gross margin. I wanted that growth to come with margins that stabilized and then expanded. Revenue has done better than I expected. Profitability has gone the other way, and Ethos looks more and more like a marketer buying growth than an insurance platform getting better at what it does.

Revenue up, bottom line flat

Year over year, adjusted EBITDA still grew, from $18.7M to $34.9M. But revenue grew 151%, so margin fell from 20.0% to 14.8%. Only about 11.5 cents of each added revenue dollar reached adjusted EBITDA.

Q4 guidance is $220-224M of revenue and $30-32M of adjusted EBITDA, about a 14% margin. Management expects the squeeze to continue.

Does revenue growth matter if they can't grow the bottom line?

Sales and marketing is over 70% of revenue

Through 2025, sales and marketing ran 58-61% of revenue. In 2026 it has been 74.6%, 67.6% and 72.0%. Q1 included a one-time $16.5M agent compensation charge, and without it Q1 was 66.1%. Q3 had no such charge. In Q3, sales and marketing grew 197% against revenue up 151%. Very little of it is stock comp. Almost all of the IPO stock comp sits in G&A.

Compared with Q3 2025, G&A and technology fell as a share of revenue and added about 6 points of margin, the way fixed costs should. Sales and marketing rose 11 points and more than wiped that out.

The 98% gross margin hides the cost of each sale

Ethos reports about a 98% gross margin because its cost of revenue is mostly underwriting data checks, about 2% of revenue. Agent payouts and advertising sit in sales and marketing instead. Those are variable costs. Every agent sale comes with an agent payout, and every direct sale needs ad spend to find the customer. That's what gross margin is supposed to capture.

Ethos also reports contribution margin, which subtracts agent payouts, ads and other per-policy costs as well. It ran 39-43% from Q4 2024 through Q4 2025. This year it has been 30.3%, 32.9% and 28.2%. That's the gross margin I care about, and it keeps falling.

Why: agents are taking over

Third-party agents brought in 24% of revenue in Q1, 39% in Q2 and 49.5% in Q3. That channel grew 209% year over year. Direct revenue is below its Q1 level ($146.0M in Q1, $118.8M in Q3).

Agents get most of the commission. Carriers pay most of a term policy's commission in the first year, as a percentage of the first-year premium, and little or nothing after that. Ethos's own agent terms start new producers at 80% of first-year premium, with higher tiers for bigger producers. Ethos's carrier contracts likely pay it more than 80% of premium, so the agent's share of what Ethos books is somewhat lower. The S-1 showed what agents took as a share of Ethos's third-party revenue:

PeriodAgents' share of third-party revenueEthos keepsBasis
202362%38%Disclosed
202468%32%Disclosed
First nine months 202470%30%Disclosed
First nine months 202558%42%Disclosed
Q3 2026~70-80%~20-30%My estimate

Working backward, if agents took 58-70% of revenue while starting at 80% of premium, Ethos was booking roughly 115-140% of first-year premium per policy (that includes expected renewals, since Ethos books lifetime commissions upfront). That's my calculation, and Ethos doesn't disclose it.

Ethos stopped breaking out the agent share after the IPO. For the Q3 estimate I started with Q3's $164.3M of variable acquisition costs from the contribution-profit reconciliation. I assumed direct sales cost 60-70% of direct revenue, which leaves $81-93M for agents and other third-party costs. Against $116.4M of third-party revenue, that's 70-80%. The direct assumption is mine and the remainder includes some other costs, so treat it as a rough range. I want the Q3 10-Q to settle it.

The per-policy numbers show the same pattern:

Q3 2025Q2 2026Q3 2026
Revenue per policy~$1,907$1,758$1,655 (-13% YoY)
Sales and marketing per policy~$1,160$1,188$1,192 (+3% YoY)
S&M share of each policy's revenue61%68%72%

Q3 2025 per-policy figures are approximate. The release gives the 13% decline but not the prior-year policy count.

Each policy costs a little more to sell and brings in less. Ethos attributes the lower revenue per policy to the shift toward third-party sales. The fastest-growing part of the business is also the least profitable part, so as long as agents outgrow direct, margins keep falling.

What Ethos actually keeps

There's a second problem with the headline growth. On an agent sale, Ethos books the carrier's full commission as revenue and then records the agent's cut as an expense. Amazon does the opposite with marketplace sellers: it counts only its fee as revenue. Ethos's method is allowed under the accounting rules because the carrier contracts with Ethos and Ethos pays the agents. But most of that revenue passes straight through to agents.

Here is Q3 on Amazon's basis, counting only what Ethos keeps from agent sales:

ReportedNet at 58% agent shareNet at 75% agent share
Q3 2026 revenue$235.2M~$168M~$148M
YoY growth151%~133%~106%
Adj. EBITDA margin14.8%~21%~24%
Q3 2025 adj. EBITDA margin, same basis20.0%~26%~26%

My estimate. Q3 2025 assumes the disclosed 58% agent share, with third-party revenue backed out of the 209% growth rate.

As agent sales become a bigger share of the mix, reported revenue growth runs ahead of what Ethos keeps. EBITDA dollars don't depend on how revenue is booked, and on a net basis margins are still falling.

The bull case

To be fair, this was a great quarter on the top line. Revenue grew 151%. Full-year guidance has climbed from $510-514M at the start of the year to $727-731M last quarter and now $838-842M. Management says new policies pay back their variable costs within about 60 days. The stock closed November 2 at $42.62 and traded around $47 after hours.

None of that answers my question. Saul's approach is finding companies where growth turns into more and more profit. I was hoping margins would stabilize this quarter. Instead the compression sped up, and the Q4 guide says it continues. Guidance has been conservative before, but the margin decline is already in three quarters of reported results.

Drew,
Heavily trimmed, leaning toward exiting
